title: Tea-colored urine
objective: Recognize rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain, weakness, dark urine, high CK) and give early, aggressive IV fluids, watching for kidney injury, hyperkalemia, compartment syndrome and DIC

brief.situation: 11:00 in a medical ICU. You are Mr. Novotny's nurse. He is 68, found on his kitchen floor this morning after a fall, probably down since last night. He takes a statin. He has just arrived from the emergency department with one liter of fluid in.
handover: He is weak and his right thigh and buttock, which he lay on, ache. A catheter is in; the first urine is dark brown.

Orders: isotonic fluid at the ordered rate, titrated to a urine output target; hourly output; a repeat potassium and CK; telemetry. A PRN ketorolac order is on the chart from the emergency department.
Unit practice: the nurse titrates fluid to the ordered output target, watches lungs and oxygen for overload, and calls the intensivist for a potassium over 6 or ECG changes.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Myoglobin and potassium load progress toward kidney injury and dysrhythmia while fluid lags. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It barely progresses with fluid titrated to output and potassium treated. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

The intensivist reassesses with repeat labs: about 30 min.

then.log: CK 46,000 U/L; potassium 6.3; creatinine 1.9 (baseline 0.9); calcium low. ECG: peaked T waves. Dipstick: large blood, urine microscopy: no red cells.
Right thigh and buttock firm and tender but not tense; foot pulses present; sensation intact. Recheck hourly.
Lungs clear, SpO2 96% on room air, no edema; 1 L in, 150 mL out.
Home statin; ketorolac PRN ordered by the emergency department; no other nephrotoxins.

effects.log: The intensivist reviews him: output on target, potassium down, compartments soft.

why.question: What is happening to his muscles and kidneys, what is the immediate danger, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and the danger
parts.criteria: Rhabdomyolysis from a long lie (CK far above 5 times normal, dark urine with blood on dipstick but no red cells); immediate danger hyperkalemia (peaked T waves); also AKI, compartment syndrome and DIC.
parts.modelAnswer: He lay on the floor all night and broke down muscle: his CK is 46,000 and his urine is dark with blood on the dipstick but no red cells, which is myoglobin. The immediate danger is his potassium of 6.3 with peaked T waves; his kidneys are already injured, and I'm watching for compartment syndrome and DIC.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Titrates isotonic fluid toward the output target while watching for overload; calls the intensivist for hyperkalemia treatment; holds the NSAID and statin; checks compartments hourly.
parts.modelAnswer: Turn the fluid up toward the output target and watch his lungs, call the intensivist now for the potassium, hold the ketorolac and statin, and check his thigh and buttock every hour.

expertPath.text: CK 46,000, potassium 6.3 with peaked T waves, creatinine doubled, dipstick blood without red cells.
Rhabdomyolysis. Call the intensivist; hold the ketorolac and statin.
Lungs clear: titrate fluid toward the output target.
Give the ordered hyperkalemia treatment; check the compartments; document hourly.

arrest.headline: Hyperkalemic arrest
arrest.body: Rhabdomyolysis releases potassium as well as myoglobin. Peaked T waves need the intensivist now, alongside aggressive fluid and no nephrotoxins.

stabilized.headline: Treated
stabilized.body: You recognized rhabdomyolysis, called within minutes for the potassium, titrated fluid to target while watching his lungs, held the nephrotoxins and checked his compartments. That is the expert path.

stabilizedGaps.headline: Stabilized, with gaps
stabilizedGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether the fluid and potassium treatment both happened, and whether the ketorolac went in.

time_up.headline: Untreated
time_up.body: Hyperkalemia from rhabdomyolysis needs treatment within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: A long lie on the floor, a CK of 46,000 (far above 5 times normal), and dark urine with blood on the dipstick but no red cells is rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria. The immediate danger is the potassium of 6.3 with peaked T waves; the creatinine has already doubled, and compartment syndrome and DIC can follow. Call the intensivist now for hyperkalemia treatment, titrate isotonic fluid toward the ordered urine output target while watching his lungs and oxygen for overload, hold the ketorolac and the statin, and check the compartments he lay on every hour.
